source: I quickly followed suit, and descending into the bar-room accosted the grinning landlord very pleasantly. I cherished no malice towards him, though he had been skylarking with me not a little in the matter of my bedfellow.

However, a good laugh is a mighty good thing, and rather too scarce a good thing; the more’s the pity. So, if any one man, in his own proper person, afford stuff for a good joke to anybody, let him not be backward, but let him cheerfully allow himself to spend and be spent in that way. And the man that has anything bountifully laughable about him, be sure there is more in that man than you perhaps think for.

The bar-room was now full of the boarders who had been dropping in the night previous, and whom I had not as yet had a good look at. They were nearly all whalemen; chief mates, and second mates, and third mates, and sea carpenters, and sea coopers, and sea blacksmiths, and harpooneers, and ship keepers; a brown and brawny company, with bosky beards; an unshorn, shaggy set, all wearing monkey jackets for morning gowns.

You could pretty plainly tell how long each one had been ashore. This young fellow’s healthy cheek is like a sun-toasted pear in hue, and would seem to smell almost as musky; he cannot have been three days landed from his Indian voyage. That man next him looks a few shades lighter; you might say a touch of satin wood is in him. In the complexion of a third still lingers a tropic tawn, but slightly bleached withal; he doubtless has tarried whole weeks ashore. But who could show a cheek like Queequeg? which, barred with various tints, seemed like the Andes’ western slope, to show forth in one array, contrasting climates, zone by zone.
“Grub, ho!” now cried the landlord, flinging open a door, and in we went to breakfast.

They say that men who have seen the world, thereby become quite at ease in manner, quite self-possessed in company. Not always, though: Ledyard, the great New England traveller, and Mungo Park, the Scotch one; of all men, they possessed the least assurance in the parlor. But perhaps the mere crossing of Siberia in a sledge drawn by dogs as Ledyard did, or the taking a long solitary walk on an empty stomach, in the negro heart of Africa, which was the sum of poor Mungo’s performances—this kind of travel, I say, may not be the very best mode of attaining a high social polish. Still, for the most part, that sort of thing is to be had anywhere.

These reflections just here are occasioned by the circumstance that after we were all seated at the table, and I was preparing to hear some good stories about whaling; to my no small surprise, nearly every man maintained a profound silence. And not only that, but they looked embarrassed. Yes, here were a set of sea-dogs, many of whom without the slightest bashfulness had boarded great whales on the high seas—entire strangers to them—and duelled them dead without winking; and yet, here they sat at a social breakfast table—all of the same calling, all of kindred tastes—looking round as sheepishly at each other as though they had never been out of sight of some sheepfold among the Green Mountains. A curious sight; these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!

But as for Queequeg—why, Queequeg sat there among them—at the head of the table, too, it so chanced; as cool as an icicle. To be sure I cannot say much for his breeding. His greatest admirer could not have cordially justified his bringing his harpoon into breakfast with him, and using it there without ceremony; reaching over the table with it, to the imminent jeopardy of many heads, and grappling the beefsteaks towards him. But that was certainly very coolly done by him, and every one knows that in most people’s estimation, to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly.

We will not speak of all Queequeg’s peculiarities here; how he eschewed coffee and hot rolls, and applied his undivided attention to beefsteaks, done rare. Enough, that when breakfast was over he withdrew like the rest into the public room, lighted his tomahawk-pipe, and was sitting there quietly digesting and smoking with his inseparable hat on, when I sallied out for a stroll.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 5 — Morgenmad
paragraphs: Jeg fulgte hurtigt efter og gik ned i værtshusstuen, hvor jeg hilste meget venligt på den grinende vært. Jeg bar ikke nag til ham, selv om han havde spillet mig adskillige puds i sagen om min sengekammerat.

Men en god latter er en gevaldig god ting og desværre en ting, der er lidt for sjælden. Så hvis nogen i egen person giver stof til en god spøg for andre, så lad ham ikke holde sig tilbage, men lad ham glad bruge sig selv og lade sig bruge på den måde. Og manden, der har noget rigeligt latterligt ved sig — du kan være sikker på, at der er mere i den mand, end du måske tror.

Værtshusstuen var nu fuld af de kostgængere, der var kommet ind en efter en aftenen før, og som jeg endnu ikke havde fået set ordentligt. De var næsten alle hvalfangere — førstestyrmænd, andenstyrmænd, tredjestyrmænd, skibstømrere, skibsbødkere, skibssmede, harpunerer og skibsvogtere. De var et brunt og kraftigt selskab med buskede skæg, en uraget, lådden flok, der alle bar sømandsjakker som morgenkåber.

Man kunne ret tydeligt se, hvor længe hver enkelt havde været i land. Denne unge mands raske kind har farve som en solbagt pære og ville næsten at dømme efter udseendet lugte lige så moskusagtigt. Han kan ikke have været tre dage hjemme fra sin rejse til Indien. Manden ved siden af ham er nogle nuancer lysere. Man kunne sige, at der er et strejf af satintræ over ham. I den tredjes ansigtsfarve hænger der endnu en tropebrun tone, om end den nu er lidt blegnet. Han har uden tvivl været i land i hele uger. Men hvem kunne vise en kind som Queequegs? Den var tværstribet med forskellige farvetoner og lignede den vestlige skråning af Andesbjergene, hvor man ser modsatte klimaer i en række, zone for zone.
»Mad, hej!« råbte værten nu og smækkede en dør op, og ind gik vi til morgenmad.

Man siger, at mænd, der har set verden, bliver helt ubesværede i deres optræden og ganske selvsikre i selskab af den grund. Men ikke altid. Ledyard, den store rejsende fra New England, og Mungo Park, den skotske, havde af alle mænd mindst selvsikkerhed i en dagligstue. Men måske er det ikke den allerbedste vej til høj selskabelig slebethed alene at krydse Sibirien i en slæde trukket af hunde, som Ledyard gjorde, eller at tage en lang, ensom gåtur på tom mave i hjertet af det sorte Afrika, hvilket var summen af stakkels Mungos bedrifter — den slags rejser, siger jeg. Alligevel kan man for det meste få den slags slebethed hvor som helst.

Disse overvejelser melder sig lige her, fordi næsten alle mændene til min ikke ringe overraskelse bevarede en dyb tavshed, efter at vi alle var kommet til bords, og jeg gjorde mig klar til at høre nogle gode historier om hvalfangst. Og ikke nok med det, de så også forlegne ud. Ja, her sad en flok søulke, hvoraf mange uden den mindste generthed var gået om bord på store hvaler på åbent hav — fuldstændig fremmede for dem — og havde duelleret dem ihjel uden at blinke. Alligevel sad de nu ved et selskabeligt morgenbord, alle af samme fag og alle med beslægtet smag, og så rundt på hinanden så fåreagtigt, som om de aldrig havde været ude af syne af en fårefold i Green Mountains. Et ejendommeligt syn — disse generte bjørne, disse frygtsomme krigerhvalfangere!

Men Queequeg sad blandt dem — for bordenden, som det nu faldt ud — kold som en istap. Om hans opdragelse kan jeg rigtignok ikke sige meget godt. Hans største beundrer kunne ikke helhjertet have forsvaret, at han tog harpunen med til morgenmad og brugte den uden videre, rakte over bordet med den, så mange hoveder var i fare, og hægtede bøfferne hen til sig. Men det gjorde han i hvert fald meget koldblodigt, og alle ved, at når de fleste skal bedømme det, er det at gøre noget koldblodigt det samme som at gøre det fint.

Vi vil ikke dvæle ved alle Queequegs særheder her — hvordan han undgik kaffe og varme rundstykker og viede al sin opmærksomhed til bøffer, kun let stegt. Det er nok at sige, at han efter morgenmaden som de andre trak sig tilbage til fællesstuen, tændte sin tomahawk-pibe og sad der roligt og fordøjede og røg med sin uadskillelige hat på, mens jeg gik ud for at tage en tur.
